subject: Accounting
title: WeWork's Fantasy Metrics
description: A quick win: understand WeWork's Fantasy Metrics.

hook.text: WeWork's IPO filing introduced 'community adjusted EBITDA'—and accountants laughed out loud.

buildup.text: Standard metrics showed massive losses. So WeWork invented its own measure that removed bad costs.

discovery.text: The creative metric stripped out marketing, general expenses, and even basic building costs.

twist.text: Investors who stuck to traditional financial statements saw the disaster coming from miles away.

climax.text: The IPO collapsed. The CEO was ousted. Standard accounting won over fantasy metrics.

punchline.text: You can rename a loss. You can't rename reality.

quiz.question: Why did WeWork's IPO fail?
options: Financial statements revealed massive losses despite creative metrics

details.summary: WeWork's IPO filing introduced 'Community Adjusted EBITDA,' a non-GAAP metric that stripped out virtually all real costs to make massive losses appear as profits. This topic examines how creative non-GAAP metrics can deceive investors.
details.whyItMatters: WeWork's collapsed IPO was a watershed moment for non-GAAP metric skepticism. It taught investors that companies creating custom profitability metrics may be hiding unsustainable economics.
takeaways: Community Adjusted EBITDA excluded building costs, corporate overhead, and marketing—virtually all expenses
WeWork reported $467 million in Community Adjusted EBITDA while losing $1.9 billion under GAAP
The SEC has since increased scrutiny of non-GAAP metrics that paint misleadingly positive pictures

faq.question: What was WeWork's Community Adjusted EBITDA?
faq.answer: It was a custom metric that removed so many costs—building expenses, headquarters overhead, and marketing—that it converted WeWork's $1.9 billion GAAP loss into a $467 million 'profit.' Investors and analysts rejected it as essentially meaningless.

faq.question: How can investors evaluate non-GAAP metrics?
faq.answer: Always check what expenses are excluded and whether they're truly non-recurring. Compare the non-GAAP number to the GAAP equivalent—a large gap is a red flag. Be skeptical of any company that creates unique metrics not used by its industry peers.
